Pulling back singularities of codimension one objects

Abstract.

We prove that the preimage of a germ of a singular analytic hypersurface under a germ of a finite holomorphic map g:(ℂn,𝟎)→(ℂn,𝟎)g:(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}) is again singular. This provides a generalization of previous results of this nature by Ebenfelt-Rothschild [3], Lebl [7], and Denkowski [2]. The same statement is proved for pullbacks of singular codimension one holomorphic foliations.

1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
32SXX,32S65,14J17

1. Introduction

This note is devoted to proving the following two theorems:

Theorem A.

Let g:(ℂn,𝟎)→(ℂn,𝟎)g:(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}) be a germ of a finite holomorphic map. Let XX be a germ of an analytic hypersurface through 𝟎{\bm{0}} that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}. Then, the germ of a hypersurface g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}.

Theorem B.

Let g:(ℂn,𝟎)→(ℂn,𝟎)g:(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}) be a germ of a finite holomorphic map. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a germ of a codimension one holomorphic foliation that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}. Then, the pullback foliation g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}.

In fact, these two theorems are equivalent; see Proposition 3.1 below.

It is important to note that Theorem A is about the ‘‘reduced structure’’ of analytic hypersurfaces and about the ‘‘set-theoretic’’ preimage---no multiplicities are taken into consideration. This causes a subtlety that is the main challenge in the proofs. In fact, the equivalence between Theorems A and B plays an important conceptual role11 1 We use it in the proof of Proposition 4.1, which is the most technical step of the proof of Theorem A. in working with the set-theoretic preimage of a hypersurface. This is because the pullback of a singular codimension one holomorphic foliation is defined in a way that ignores the multiplicities arising from the critical hypersurfaces of gg; see Section 2.3.

When XX is a germ of an analytic subvariety of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} having arbitrary dimension, a version of Theorem A has been proved by Ebenfelt-Rothschild [3, Theorem 2.1], Lebl [7, Section 4], and Denkowski [2, Theorem 1.2] under the additional hypothesis that the Jacobian det⁡(D​g){\rm det}(Dg) does not vanish identically on g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X). However, this hypothesis has been removed in the case that dim⁡(X)=1{\rm dim}(X)=1, see [3, Theorem 4.1] and [7, Section 4]. We refer the reader to the aforementioned papers for further details.

Surprisingly, until now, the statement of Theorem A seems to be open in the case that det⁡(D​g){\rm det}(Dg) is allowed to vanish identically on g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X).

Note also that a version of Theorem B was proved in dimension 22 by Kaschner, Pérez, and the second author of the present paper in [6, Lemma 2.4].

In Section 2 we give background on finite holomorphic maps, analytic hypersurfaces, and singular codimension one holomorphic foliations. Section 3 is devoted to proving that Theorems A and B are equivalent. We conclude the proof of both theorems by presenting a proof of Theorem A in Section 4.

Notational Conventions:
Germs and their representatives will often be used interchangeably as a minor abuse of notation. The notation g:(U,0)→(V,0)g:(U,0)\rightarrow(V,0) when used for gg that is not a germ means that g:U→Vg:U\rightarrow V is the map and g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0.

2. Background

2.1. Finite Maps

A holomorphic germ g:(ℂn,𝟎)→(ℂn,𝟎)g:(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}) is finite if g−1​(𝟎)∩U={𝟎}g^{-1}({\bm{0}})\cap U=\{{\bm{0}}\} for a sufficiently small neighborhood UU of 𝟎{\bm{0}} and some representative gg. Note that this implies that if 𝒚{\bm{y}} is sufficiently close to 𝟎{\bm{0}} then g−1​(𝒚)∩Ug^{-1}({\bm{y}})\cap U is a finite set. The following lemma is well-known:

Lemma 2.1.

Let g:(ℂn,𝟎)→(ℂn,𝟎)g:(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}) be a germ of a finite holomorphic map. Then, there are arbitrarily small neighborhoods U,WU,W of 𝟎{\bm{0}} and a representative g:(U,𝟎)→(W,𝟎)g:(U,{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(W,{\bm{0}}) of the germ that is proper.

We refer the reader to [9, Theorem 15.1.6] for a proof of Lemma 2.1. We also refer the reader to [5, p. 667-670] for various additional properties of finite maps.

2.2. Hypersurfaces

We refer the reader to the monograph by Milnor [8] for more details than will be presented here. Let UU be an open neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}} in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. The term hypersurface in UU will refer to a potentially reducible analytic subset of UU, each of whose irreducible components has codimension one. Throughout this paper we will be interested in the “reduced structure” of a hypersurface, thinking of it as an analytic set rather than a divisor.

Note that if XX is a reducible germ of a hypersurface at 𝟎{\bm{0}} then XX is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}. Moreover, reducibility is preserved under preimage by gg. Therefore, it suffices to prove Theorem A for irreducible germs, and most of our attention will be focused on them.

Associated to any irreducible hypersurface XX in UU is a holomorphic function ψ:U→ℂ\psi:U\rightarrow\mathbb{C} that is prime in the ring of germs of holomorphic functions 𝒪ℂn,𝟎\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}} such that

(1) X={𝐱∈U:ψ(𝐱)=0}andd​ψ≢0 on X.\displaystyle X=\{{\bf x}\in U\,:\,\psi({\bf x})=0\}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mbox{$d\psi\not\equiv 0$ on $X$}.

The condition that d​ψ≢0d\psi\not\equiv 0 on XX follows from ψ\psi being a prime element of 𝒪ℂn,𝟎\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}} and it ensures that ψ\psi vanishes to order one on the smooth part of XX. In other words, the Cartier divisor (ψ)(\psi) defines the reduced divisor associated to XX.

Lemma 2.2.

Suppose XX is an irreducible hypersurface passing through 𝟎{\bm{0}} that is given by (1). If XX is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}} then there is a smaller neighborhood U′⊂UU^{\prime}\subset U of 𝟎{\bm{0}} in which the singular locus of XX is given by

Xsing={𝒙∈U′:d​ψ​(𝒙)=0},\displaystyle X_{\rm sing}=\{{\bm{x}}\in U^{\prime}\,:\,d\psi({\bm{x}})=0\},

where dd denotes the exterior derivative.

Proof.

We have,

Xsing={𝒙∈U:ψ⁡(x)=0​ and ​d​ψ​(𝒙)=0}.\displaystyle X_{\rm sing}=\{{\bm{x}}\in U\,:\,\psi(x)=0\mbox{ and }d\psi({\bm{x}})=0\}.

Let

S={𝒙∈U:d​ψ​(𝒙)=0}.\displaystyle S=\{{\bm{x}}\in U\,:\,d\psi({\bm{x}})=0\}.

We can choose U′⊂UU^{\prime}\subset U to be sufficiently small so that each irreducible component of S∩U′S\cap U^{\prime} passes through 𝟎{\bm{0}}. For the remainder of the proof we will work entirely in U′U^{\prime}.

It remains to show that ψ|S​(𝒙)≡0\psi|_{S}({{\bm{x}}})\equiv 0. This is trivial if S={𝟎}S=\{{\bm{0}}\}. Otherwise, let S0S_{0} be an irreducible component of SS. The smooth locus S0,regS_{0,{\rm reg}} is a submanifold of U′U^{\prime} that is dense in S0S_{0}. Any two points p,q∈S0,regp,q\in S_{0,{\rm reg}} can be connected by a smooth path γ:[0,1]→S0,reg\gamma:[0,1]\rightarrow S_{0,{\rm reg}} and

ψ⁡(q)−ψ⁡(p)=∫γ𝑑ψ=0.\displaystyle\psi(q)-\psi(p)=\int_{\gamma}d\psi=0.

Therefore ψ\psi is constant on S0,regS_{0,{\rm reg}} and hence on S0S_{0}. As S0S_{0} passes through 𝟎{\bm{0}} and ψ⁡(𝟎)=0\psi({\bm{0}})=0, ψ\psi vanishes on S0S_{0}. ∎

2.3. Singular codimension one holomorphic foliations

We refer the reader to the survey paper by Cerveau [1] for more background than we will present here. A singular codimension one holomorphic foliation ℱ\mathcal{F} in a sufficiently small neighborhood UU of 𝟎{\bm{0}} in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} can be described by a holomorphic one form ω\omega having the following two properties:

  • (i)

    ω∧d​ω=0\omega\wedge d\omega=0 (integrability), and

  • (ii)

    ωsing:={𝒙∈U:ω⁡(𝒙)=0}\omega_{\rm sing}:=\{{\bm{x}}\in U\,:\,\omega({\bm{x}})=0\} has codimension ≥2\geq 2.

It is a consequence of the Frobenius Theorem that any 𝒙∈U∖ωsing{\bm{x}}\in U\setminus\omega_{\rm sing} has a neighborhood NN in which there is a system of holomorphic coordinates 𝒛=(z1,…,zn){\bm{z}}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) on NN such that ω=u⁡(𝒛)​d​z1\omega=u({\bm{z}})dz_{1} with u⁡(𝒛)≠0u({\bm{z}})\neq 0 on NN (i.e. uu is a unit). In these coordinates, the tangent planes to Ker⁡(ω){\rm Ker}(\omega) become the “vertical hyperplanes” {z1=const}\{z_{1}={\rm const}\}. They are interpreted as local leaves of ℱ\mathcal{F} in the local coordinate 𝒛{\bm{z}}. By transporting them back to the original coordinate 𝒚\bm{y} and gluing, one obtains global leaves of ℱ\mathcal{F} on U∖ωsingU\setminus\omega_{\rm sing}. One calls ωsing\omega_{\rm sing} the singular locus of ℱ\mathcal{F} and denotes it by ℱsing\mathcal{F}_{\rm sing}.

Occasionally, and only when there is no ambiguity, we will use the term “foliation” to mean “singular codimension one holomorphic foliation”.

Let U,W⊂ℂnU,W\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} be open sets and let g:U→Wg:U\rightarrow W be a finite holomorphic mapping. Suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is a singular codimension one holomorphic foliation that is defined on WW by a holomorphic one form ω\omega (satisfying (i) and (ii)). Then, one defines the pullback g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} on UU by a holomorphic one form g#​ωg^{\#}\omega on UU obtained by dividing g∗​ωg^{*}\omega by a suitable holomorphic function, in order that the zero locus of g#​ωg^{\#}\omega is of codimension two or larger.22 2 The notation g#​ωg^{\#}\omega is non-standard and the reader should note that it is only well-defined up to multiplication by a non-vanishing holomorphic function. Because pullback g∗g^{*} respects wedge product and exterior derivatives, g∗​ωg^{*}\omega still satisfies (i), and a simple calculation shows that (i) continues to hold after rescaling g∗​ωg^{*}\omega to obtain g#​ωg^{\#}\omega. Meanwhile, the rescaling was done so that g#​ωg^{\#}\omega satisfies (ii).

Remark 2.3.

It is possible that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} be singular at 𝒙\bm{x} even though ℱ\mathcal{F} is regular at g⁡(𝒙)g(\bm{x}). For example, in dimension two, if ω=d​y1\omega=dy_{1} and g⁡(x1,x2)=(x12−x22,x2)g(x_{1},x_{2})=(x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2},x_{2}), then

g∗​ω=d⁡(x12−x22)=2​x1​d​x1−2​x2​d​x2=g#​ω,\displaystyle g^{*}\omega=d(x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2})=2x_{1}dx_{1}-2x_{2}dx_{2}=g^{\#}\omega,

which vanishes at (0,0)(0,0).

It is immediate from the definition that in a sufficiently small neighborhood NN of any regular point for gg the pullback g∗g^{*} sends local leaves of ℱ\mathcal{F} in g⁡(N)g(N) to local leaves of g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} in NN. The following lemma justifies that this also happens more generally:

Lemma 2.4.

Suppose that 𝐱{\bm{x}} is a regular point for g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} and g⁡(𝐱)g({\bm{x}}) is a regular point for ℱ\mathcal{F}. Then, there exists a neighborhood NN of 𝐱{\bm{x}} such that if LL is the local leaf of ℱ\mathcal{F} through g⁡(𝐱)g({\bm{x}}) in g⁡(N)g(N) then g−1​(L)g^{-1}(L) is the local leaf of g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} through 𝐱{\bm{x}} in NN.

Proof.

Since g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is regular at 𝒙{\bm{x}} and ℱ\mathcal{F} is regular at g⁡(𝒙)g({\bm{x}}) we can choose a connected neighborhood NN of 𝒙\bm{x} sufficiently small so that:

  • (a)

    there is a system of local coordinates (z1,…,zn)(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) in NN in which local leaves of g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} are given by vertical hyperplanes {z1=const}\{z_{1}={\rm const}\}, and

  • (b)

    there is a system of local coordinates (w1,…,wn)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}) in g⁡(N)g(N) in which ℱ\mathcal{F} is given by vertical hyperplanes {w1=const}\{w_{1}={\rm const}\}.

Let N0⊂N∖crit⁡(g)N_{0}\subset N\setminus{\rm crit}(g) be an open set. (Remark that since gg is finite it is an open mapping [9, Theorem 15.1.6] implying that crit⁡(g){\rm crit}(g) is a proper analytic subvariety of NN.) Then, gg sends local leaves of g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} within N0N_{0} to local leaves of ℱ\mathcal{F} within g⁡(N0)g(N_{0}). Therefore, if we write

(w1,…,wn)=g⁡(z1,…,zn)=(g1​(z1,…,zn),…,gn​(z1,…,zn)),\displaystyle(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n})=g(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})=(g_{1}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}),\ldots,g_{n}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})),

then within N0N_{0} we have that g1​(z1,…,zn)g_{1}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) is independent of z2,…,znz_{2},\ldots,z_{n}, i.e.

g1​(z1,…,zn)≡g1​(z1).\displaystyle g_{1}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\equiv g_{1}(z_{1}).

Because NN is connected, this property carries over to gg within all of NN. In particular, gg sends every local leaf of g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} in NN to some local leaf of ℱ\mathcal{F} in g⁡(N)g(N).

We can then choose a smaller neighborhood N′⊂NN^{\prime}\subset N so that the local leaf of g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} through 𝒙{\bm{x}} is the only local leaf of g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} within N′N^{\prime} whose image contains g⁡(𝒙)g({\bm{x}}). ∎

3. Equivalence of Theorems A and B

Proposition 3.1.

Theorem A holds if and only if Theorem B holds.

Proof.

It suffices to show that the following are equivalent:

  • (a)

    There is a germ of an irreducible hypersurface XX that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}} such that g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is smooth, and

  • (b)

    There is a germ of a singular codimension one holomorphic foliation ℱ\mathcal{F} that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}} such that g∗​(ℱ)g^{*}(\mathcal{F}) is smooth.

Suppose (a) in order to prove (b). Suppose WW is a neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}} in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} and XX is an irreducible hypersurface in WW given by

X={𝒚∈W:ψ⁡(𝒚)=0}andd​ψ≢0 on X,\displaystyle X=\{{{\bm{y}}}\in W\,:\,\psi({{\bm{y}}})=0\}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mbox{$d\psi\not\equiv 0$ on $X$},

with 𝟎∈Xsing{\bm{0}}\in X_{\rm sing}. Lemma 2.2 allows us to shrink to a smaller neighborhood W′⊂WW^{\prime}\subset W of 𝟎{\bm{0}} so that

Xsing={𝒚∈W′:d​ψ​(𝒚)=0}.\displaystyle X_{\rm sing}=\{{\bm{y}}\in W^{\prime}\,:\,d\psi({\bm{y}})=0\}.

Since XsingX_{\rm sing} has codimension two or larger in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}, the one form d​ψd\psi defines a singular codimension one holomorphic foliation ℱ\mathcal{F} on W′W^{\prime} with 𝟎∈ℱsing=Xsing{\bm{0}}\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm sing}=X_{\rm sing}.

By hypothesis, g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is smooth, so we can choose holomorphic coordinates (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) in a neighborhood UU of 𝟎{\bm{0}} so that g−1(X)={x1=0}g^{-1}(X)=\{x_{1}=0\}. Therefore ψ∘g⁡(𝒙)=x1m​u​(𝒙)\psi\circ g({\bm{x}})=x_{1}^{m}u({\bm{x}}) for some integer m≥1m\geq 1 and some unit (non-vanishing holomorphic function) u⁡(𝒙)u({\bm{x}}). Hence,

(2) g∗​(d​ψ)=d⁡(g∗​ψ)=d⁡(ψ∘g⁡(𝒙))=d⁡(x1m​u​(𝒙))=m​x1m−1​d​x1​u​(𝒙)+x1m​d​u​(𝒙).\displaystyle g^{*}(d\psi)=d(g^{*}\psi)=d(\psi\circ g({\bm{x}}))=d(x_{1}^{m}u({\bm{x}}))=mx_{1}^{m-1}dx_{1}u({\bm{x}})+x_{1}^{m}du({\bm{x}}).

Recall that the pullback g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is defined in a neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}} by any holomorphic one form g#​(d​ψ)g^{\#}(d\psi) obtained by rescaling g∗​(d​ψ)g^{*}(d\psi) in order that the zero locus of g#​(d​ψ)g^{\#}(d\psi) is of codimension two or larger. In this case, one can use

(3) g#​(d​ψ):=1x1m−1​g∗​(d​ψ)=m​u​(𝒙)​d​x1+x1​d​u​(𝒙).\displaystyle g^{\#}(d\psi):=\frac{1}{x_{1}^{m-1}}g^{*}(d\psi)=m\ u({\bm{x}})dx_{1}+x_{1}du({\bm{x}}).

Note that g#​(d​ψ)​(𝟎)=m​u​(𝟎)​d​x1≠0g^{\#}(d\psi)({\bm{0}})=m\ u({\bm{0}})dx_{1}\neq 0, so that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is smooth in some neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}}, thus proving (b).

We now prove that (b) implies (a). Suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is a singular codimension one holomorphorphic foliation that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}} and that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is smooth in some neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}}. We will use the hypothesis that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is smooth to prove that ℱ\mathcal{F} is locally given by level hypersurfaces {ψ(𝒚)=const}\{\psi({\bm{y}})={\rm const}\} for a suitable holomorphic function ψ\psi. Supposing that ψ⁡(𝟎)=0\psi({\bm{0}})=0, this will produce for us an irreducible singular hypersurface X=ψ−1​(0)X=\psi^{-1}(0) whose preimage under gg is smooth.

More specifically, suppose that ℱ\mathcal{F} is given in some neighborhood W0W_{0} of 𝟎{\bm{0}} by the holomorphic one form ω\omega satisfying (i) and (ii) from the definition of foliation. Because of the hypothesis that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is smooth in a neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}}, we can do a local holomorphic change of variables so that in some neighborhood U0U_{0} of 𝟎{\bm{0}} we have that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is given by d​x1dx_{1}. In other words, g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is given by the family of vertical hyperplanes of the form {x1=const}\{x_{1}={\rm const}\} within U0U_{0}.

By Lemma 2.1 we can choose neighborhoods U⊂U0U\subset U_{0} and W⊂W0W\subset W_{0} of the origin in domain and codomain, respectively, so that g:U→Wg:U\rightarrow W is a proper map and so that g−1​(𝟎)∩W=𝟎g^{-1}({\bm{0}})\cap W={\bm{0}}. Let us also suppose that UU and WW are connected. Let δ\delta denote the topological degree of this mapping (number of preimages of a point, when counted with multiplicity). Let π1:U→ℂ\pi_{1}:U\rightarrow\mathbb{C} be projection onto the first coordinate, π1​(𝒙)=x1\pi_{1}({\bm{x}})=x_{1}. Since g:U→Wg:U\rightarrow W is proper, we can take the pushforward ψ⁡(𝒚):=g∗​π1​(𝒚)\psi({\bm{y}}):=g_{*}\pi_{1}({\bm{y}}), which is a holomorphic function on WW defined by

ψ⁡(𝒚):=(g∗​π1)​(𝒚)=∑𝒙∈g−1​(𝒚)π1​(𝒙),\displaystyle\psi({\bm{y}}):=\left(g_{*}\pi_{1}\right)({\bm{y}})=\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in g^{-1}({\bm{y}})}\pi_{1}({\bm{x}}),

where preimages are counted with multiplicities. (Remark that in certain contexts from algebraic geometry the proper pushforward is called the “trace map”; see, for example, [5, p. 668].)

We claim that level hypersurfaces of ψ\psi are tangent to leaves of ℱ\mathcal{F} at those places where both are regular. This will hold if and only if

(4) d​ψ∧ω=0on W,\displaystyle d\psi\wedge\omega=0\quad\mbox{on $W$},

which is equivalent to the kernels of both d​ψd\psi and ω\omega being parallel. Because d​ψ∧ωd\psi\wedge\omega is a holomorphic two-form and WW is connected, it suffices to check (4) on any open subset of WW.

Let NN be a simply-connected open subset of WW that is disjoint from the critical value locus, so that the Inverse Function Theorem and Monodromy Theorem allow us to construct δ\delta holomorphic inverse branches h1,…,hδ:N→Uh_{1},\ldots,h_{\delta}:N\rightarrow U of gg. Because g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is given by d​x1dx_{1}, we have that

π1∘hℓ​(𝒚)is constant on γ∩N\displaystyle\pi_{1}\circ h_{\ell}({\bm{y}})\quad\mbox{is constant on $\gamma\cap N$}

for any leaf γ\gamma of ℱ\mathcal{F} and any 1≤ℓ≤δ1\leq\ell\leq\delta. This implies that ψ\psi is constant on γ∩N\gamma\cap N and thus that d​ψ∧ω=0d\psi\wedge\omega=0 on the open set N⊂WN\subset W.

It is possible from the definition of ψ\psi that d​ψd\psi vanishes on some hypersurfaces. Let η\eta be a holomorphic one-form obtained by dividing d​ψd\psi by a suitable holomorphic function in order that the zero locus of η\eta has codimension two or larger.

Let XX be the connected33 3 A priori, XX could be a reducible hypersurface. We’ll rule this out in the last paragraph of the proof. component of

{𝒚∈W:ψ⁡(𝒚)=0}\displaystyle\{{\bm{y}}\in W\,:\,\psi({\bm{y}})=0\}

that contains 𝟎{\bm{0}}. We claim that XX is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}} and g−1(X)={x1=0}g^{-1}(X)=\{x_{1}=0\}, so that g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is smooth.

Suppose for contradiction that XX is smooth at 𝟎{\bm{0}}. Then, possibly after restricting to a smaller neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}}, we can choose a suitable local coordinate 𝒛{\bm{z}} in which X={z1=0}X=\{z_{1}=~0\}. This implies that in this coordinate ψ⁡(𝒛)=z1n​u​(𝒛)\psi({\bm{z}})=z_{1}^{n}u({\bm{z}}) for some unit u⁡(𝒛)u({\bm{z}}). The same calculation as in (2) and (3) can then be used to show that η⁡(𝟎)≠0\eta({\bm{0}})\neq 0 and hence that ℱ\mathcal{F} is smooth at 𝟎{\bm{0}}, contrary to our hypothesis.

Meanwhile, the smooth locus XregX_{\rm reg} is a leaf of ℱ\mathcal{F}. Since g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is given by the vertical leaves {x1=const}\{x_{1}={\rm const}\}, Lemma 2.4 gives that each point 𝒚∈Xreg{\bm{y}}\in X_{\rm reg} has a neighborhood in XregX_{\rm reg} each of whose preimages under gg is contained in one of the vertical leaves {x1=const}\{x_{1}={\rm const}\}. However, since XregX_{\rm reg} is dense in XX and since g−1​(𝟎)={𝟎}g^{-1}({\bm{0}})=\{{\bm{0}}\} we conclude that g−1(X)={x1=0}g^{-1}(X)=\{x_{1}=0\}. Finally, remark that if XX were reducible, then g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) would also be reducible, contradicting the conclusion of the previous sentence.

∎

4. Proof of Theorems A and B

In Proposition 3.1 we saw that Theorems A and B are equivalent. Therefore, it suffices to prove Theorem A, and we will focus entirely on that for the remainder of the paper. Let us start with two propositions.

Proposition 4.1.

Let g:(ℂn,𝟎)→(ℂn,𝟎)g:(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}) be a germ of a finite holomorphic map. Let XX be a germ of an analytic hypersurface that has an isolated singularity at 𝟎{\bm{0}}. Then, the preimage g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}.

Remark 4.2.

A version of this was proved for ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} in [6, Lemma 2.4] and the proof below extends what was done there to higher dimensions by using the algebraic technique of Koszul complexes.

Proof.

If XX is reducible at 𝟎{\bm{0}} then g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is also, and hence g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}.

Now suppose for contradiction that XX is an irreducible analytic hypersurface defined in a neighborhood WW of 𝟎{\bm{0}} and singular only at 𝟎{\bm{0}}, with the property that g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is smooth. In this one step of the proof of Theorem A, it will be convenient to use Proposition 3.1 to replace XX with a singular codimension one holomorphic foliation ℱ\mathcal{F} that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}} whose pullback g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is smooth. Moreover, in the proof of Proposition 3.1 we saw that the resulting foliation satisfies ℱsing=Xsing\mathcal{F}_{\rm sing}=X_{\rm sing}, so that 𝟎{\bm{0}} is an isolated singularity for ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Let us write gg in coordinates as g⁡(x1,…,xn)=(g1​(x1,…,xn),…,gn​(x1,…,xn))g(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=(g_{1}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),\ldots,g_{n}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})). Suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is given in a neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}} by the holomorphic one form

ω=∑i=1nai​(𝒚)​d​yi.\displaystyle\omega=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}({\bm{y}})dy_{i}.

Remark that the assumption that ℱ\mathcal{F} has an isolated singularity at 𝟎{\bm{0}} implies that the common zero set of the ai​(𝒚)a_{i}({\bm{y}}) is the origin, in other words the ai​(𝒚)a_{i}({\bm{y}}) for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n form a regular sequence in the ring of germs of holomorphic functions 𝒪ℂn,𝟎\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}.

Suppose for contradiction that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is smooth in a neighborhood of 𝟎{\bm{0}}. Then, after a suitable change of variables in the domain, we can suppose that g∗​ℱg^{*}\mathcal{F} is given by g#​ω=d​x1g^{\#}\omega=dx_{1}. In other words, if we write

g∗​ω=∑ℓ=1nbℓ​(𝒙)​d​xℓ,\displaystyle g^{*}\omega=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}b_{\ell}({\bm{x}})dx_{\ell},

then

(5) bℓ​(𝒙)=∑i=1nai​(g⁡(𝒙))​∂gi∂xℓ≡0for 2≤ℓ≤n.\displaystyle b_{\ell}({\bm{x}})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}(g({\bm{x}}))\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial x_{\ell}}\equiv 0\quad\mbox{for $2\leq\ell\leq n$.}

(Remark that one could have b1​(𝒙)≢1b_{1}({\bm{x}})\not\equiv 1 as pull-back of foliations allows one to eliminate common factors.)

Consider the holomorphic one form

η=∑i=1nai​(g⁡(𝒙))​d​xi.\displaystyle\eta=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}(g({\bm{x}}))dx_{i}.

We will now interpret (5) in terms of the Koszul Complex obtained by wedging with η\eta:

0⟶𝒪ℂn,𝟎⟶∧ηΩℂn,𝟎1⟶∧ηΩℂn,𝟎2⟶∧η⋯⟶∧ηΩℂn,𝟎n−2⟶∧ηΩℂn,𝟎n−1⟶∧ηΩℂn,𝟎n⟶0.\displaystyle 0\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge\eta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge\eta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{2}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge\eta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\cdots\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge\eta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{n-2}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge\eta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{n-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge\eta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{n}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}\longrightarrow 0.

Since gg is a finite map, the ai​(g​(𝒙))a_{i}(g({\bm{x}})) for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n also form a regular sequence in 𝒪ℂn,𝟎\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}. Therefore, the homology of the Koszul Complex vanishes in the second to last place (at the term Ωℂn,𝟎n−1\Omega^{n-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}). See, for example, [4, Theorem A2.49].

For each 2≤ℓ≤n2\leq\ell\leq n consider τℓ∈Ωℂn,𝟎n−1\tau_{\ell}\in\Omega^{n-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}} given by

(6) τℓ:=∑i=1n(−1)n−i​∂gi∂xℓ​d​x1∧⋯∧d​xi^∧⋯∧d​xn.\displaystyle\tau_{\ell}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial x_{\ell}}dx_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_{i}}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{n}.

Here, the hat on d​xi^\widehat{dx_{i}} denotes that the d​xidx_{i} has been omitted from the monomial. Condition (5) implies that

τℓ∧η=0.\displaystyle\tau_{\ell}\wedge\eta=0.

As the homology of the Koszul Complex vanishes in the second to last place, there exists αℓ∈Ωℂn,𝟎n−2\alpha_{\ell}\in\Omega^{n-2}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}} with

αℓ∧η=τℓ.\displaystyle\alpha_{\ell}\wedge\eta=\tau_{\ell}.

Let us write

αℓ=∑1≤j<k≤ncℓj,k​(𝒙)​d​x1∧⋯∧d​xj^∧⋯∧d​xk^∧⋯∧d​xn,\displaystyle\alpha_{\ell}=\sum_{1\leq j<k\leq n}c_{\ell}^{j,k}({\bm{x}})dx_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_{j}}\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_{k}}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{n},

where cℓj,k∈𝒪ℂn,𝟎c_{\ell}^{j,k}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}}.

Computing αℓ∧η\alpha_{\ell}\wedge\eta and comparing the coefficients with (6) we find that

(7) ∂g1∂xℓ\displaystyle\frac{\partial g_{1}}{\partial x_{\ell}} =∑k=2n(−1)n−k​cℓ1,k​(𝒙)​ak​(g⁡(𝒙)),\displaystyle=\sum_{k=2}^{n}(-1)^{n-k}c_{\ell}^{1,k}({\bm{x}})a_{k}(g({\bm{x}})),
∂gi∂xℓ\displaystyle\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial x_{\ell}} =∑j=1i−1(−1)n−1−jcℓj,i(𝒙)aj(g(𝒙))+∑k=i+1n(−1)n−kcℓi,k(𝒙)ak(g(𝒙))for 2≤i≤n−1, and\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(-1)^{n-1-j}c_{\ell}^{j,i}({\bm{x}})a_{j}(g({\bm{x}}))+\sum_{k=i+1}^{n}(-1)^{n-k}c_{\ell}^{i,k}({\bm{x}})a_{k}(g({\bm{x}}))\quad\mbox{for $2\leq i\leq n-1$, and}
∂gn∂xℓ\displaystyle\frac{\partial g_{n}}{\partial x_{\ell}} =∑j=1n−1(−1)n−1−j​cℓj,n​(𝒙)​aj​(g⁡(𝒙)).\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(-1)^{n-1-j}c_{\ell}^{j,n}({\bm{x}})a_{j}(g({\bm{x}})).

All we will need from (7) is that for each 2≤ℓ≤n2\leq\ell\leq n and 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n there exist some eℓi,m∈𝒪ℂn,𝟎e_{\ell}^{i,m}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}} for 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n such that

We will obtain a contradiction from (8) and the naive idea behind it will be that the left hand side of (8) should vanish to lower order than the right hand side because of the partial derivative. We will now make this idea rigorous.

Because gg is a finite map we have that gm​(0,x2,…,xn)≢0g_{m}(0,x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\not\equiv 0 for all but at most one coordinate mm. Let m1,…,mpm_{1},\ldots,m_{p} be precisely the coordinates for which this holds (either p=n−1p=n-1 or p=np=n). For each 1≤q≤p1\leq q\leq p we can write

gmq​(𝒙)=x1​gmq1​(𝒙)+gmq2​(x2,…,xm)\displaystyle g_{m_{q}}({\bm{x}})=x_{1}g_{m_{q}}^{1}({\bm{x}})+g_{m_{q}}^{2}(x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})

with gmq1∈𝒪ℂn,𝟎g_{m_{q}}^{1}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}} and gmq2∈𝒪ℂn−1,𝟎g_{m_{q}}^{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n-1},{\bm{0}}} such that gmq2​(x2,…,xm)≢0g_{m_{q}}^{2}(x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})\not\equiv 0. Let x2d2⋯xndnx_{2}^{d_{2}}\cdots x_{n}^{d_{n}} be one such monomial of this total degree. It may occur for multiple choices of qq and, without loss of generality, we can assume it occurs for q=1q=1. Proposition 4.3.

Let U,W⊂ℂnU,W\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} be neighborhoods of 𝟎{\bm{0}} and suppose g:(U,𝟎)→(W,𝟎)g:(U,{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(W,{\bm{0}}) is a finite holomorphic map, X⊂WX\subset W is an irreducible hypersurface that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}} and has singular locus XsingX_{\rm sing} of positive dimension (passing through the origin), and g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is smooth.

Then there exists open sets U′⊂UU^{\prime}\subset U and W′⊂WW^{\prime}\subset W with g⁡(U′)=W′g(U^{\prime})=W^{\prime} and a hyperplane HH in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} such that:

  1. (1)

    X∩HX\cap H is a singular hypersurface within H∩W′H\cap W^{\prime},

  2. (2)

    g−1​(H)g^{-1}(H) is smooth within U′U^{\prime}, and

  3. (3)

    g−1​(X∩H)g^{-1}(X\cap H) is a smooth hypersurface in g−1​(H)∩U′g^{-1}(H)\cap U^{\prime}.

Proof.

There is a holomorphic ψ:W→ℂ\psi:W\rightarrow\mathbb{C} such that

(9) X={𝒚∈W:ψ(𝒚)=0}andd​ψ≢0 on X.\displaystyle X=\{{\bm{y}}\in W\,:\,\psi({\bm{y}})=0\}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mbox{$d\psi\not\equiv 0$ on $X$}.

Let S⊂XS\subset X be an irreducible component of XsingX_{\rm sing} of maximal dimension

1≤k:=dim⁡(S)≤n−2.\displaystyle 1\leq k:={\rm dim}(S)\leq n-2.

Let VV be an irreducible component of g−1​(S)g^{-1}(S). Since gg is a finite map dim⁡(V)=k{\rm dim}(V)~=~k and dim⁡(g−1​(Ssing))<k{\rm dim}(g^{-1}(S_{\rm sing}))<k. Therefore, Vreg∖g−1​(Ssing)V_{\rm reg}\setminus g^{-1}(S_{\rm sing}) is an open dense subset of VV. We can therefore find a point p0∈Vreg∖g−1​(Ssing)p_{0}\in V_{\rm reg}\setminus g^{-1}(S_{\rm sing}) and an open neighborhood U′U^{\prime} of p0p_{0} in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} such that U′∩VU^{\prime}\cap V is contained in VregV_{\rm reg} and W′:=g⁡(U′)W^{\prime}:=g(U^{\prime}) satisfies that W′∩Xsing⊂SregW^{\prime}\cap X_{\rm sing}\subset S_{\rm reg}. Remark that W′W^{\prime} is an open neighborhood of g⁡(p0)g(p_{0}) because gg is also an open mapping [9, Theorem 15.1.6].

The remainder of the proof will take place within the neighborhoods U′U^{\prime} and W′W^{\prime}. By abuse of notation we will now refer to gg as the surjective finite holomorphic mapping g:U′→W′g:U^{\prime}\rightarrow W^{\prime}, refer to XX as a singular hypersurface in W′W^{\prime} whose singular locus Xsing=SX_{\rm sing}=S is a smooth manifold of dimension kk in W′W^{\prime}, and refer to VV as a smooth manifold of dimension kk in U′U^{\prime} satisfying g⁡(V)⊂Sg(V)\subset S.

For any non-constant holomorphic curve γ:𝔻→U′\gamma:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow U^{\prime} we have that D​g​(γ⁡(t))​γ′​(t)≠𝟎Dg(\gamma(t))\gamma^{\prime}(t)~\neq~{\bm{0}} for generic t∈𝔻t\in\mathbb{D}, since otherwise g⁡(γ⁡(𝔻))g(\gamma(\mathbb{D})) would be a single point. Since VV is a smooth manifold of dimension k>0k>0 we can suppose γ⁡(𝔻)⊂V\gamma(\mathbb{D})\subset V and that allows us to find a point p1∈Vp_{1}\in V and a tangent vector 𝒗1∈Tp1​V{\bm{v}}_{1}\in T_{p_{1}}V such that 𝒘1:=D​g​(p1)​𝒗1∈Tg⁡(p1)​S{\bm{w}}_{1}:=Dg(p_{1}){\bm{v}}_{1}\in T_{g(p_{1})}S is non-zero.

Let H0H_{0} be a hyperplane through g⁡(p1)g(p_{1}) that is transverse to 𝒘1{\bm{w}}_{1}. By definition, this implies that H0H_{0} is transverse to SS and to the map gg. Let LL be the line through g⁡(p1)g(p_{1}) in the direction of 𝒘1{\bm{w}}_{1}. Denote by HtH_{t} the one-parameter family of hyperplanes parallel to H0H_{0}, which we can parameterize by the intersection point t∈Ht∩Lt\in H_{t}\cap L. As transversality is an open condition, we can reduce the neighborhoods U′U^{\prime} and W′=g⁡(U′)W^{\prime}=g(U^{\prime}) so that each member of HtH_{t} is transverse to both SS and gg. Without loss of generality, we can suppose the parameter tt varies over the unit disc 𝔻\mathbb{D}.

We will now select the desired hyperplane HH satisfying Properties (1-3) from this family HtH_{t}. Since each HtH_{t} is transverse to gg we have that g−1​(Ht)g^{-1}(H_{t}) is a smooth submanifold of U′U^{\prime} so that (2) holds for all choices of tt.

We will now show that Property (1) holds for all parameters tt outside of a zero measure subset of 𝔻\mathbb{D}. Let τ:W′→𝔻\tau:W^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathbb{D} be the function that assigns to each 𝒚{\bm{y}} the value of the parameter tt such that 𝒚∈Ht{\bm{y}}\in H_{t}. Sard’s Theorem gives that the critical values of τ|Xreg\tau|_{X_{\rm reg}} form a measure zero set 𝔻0⊂𝔻\mathbb{D}_{0}\subset\mathbb{D}. For any t∈𝔻∖𝔻0t\in\mathbb{D}\setminus\mathbb{D}_{0} we have that HtH_{t} is transversal to XregX_{\rm reg}. At each 𝒚∈Xreg{\bm{y}}\in X_{\rm reg} we have

Ker⁡(d​ψ​(𝒚))=T𝒚​Xreg.\displaystyle{\rm Ker}(d\psi({\bm{y}}))=T_{\bm{y}}X_{\rm reg}.

This implies that if t∈𝔻∖𝔻0t\in\mathbb{D}\setminus\mathbb{D}_{0} then d⁡(ψ|Ht)≠0d(\psi|_{H_{t}})\neq 0 at every point of Xreg∩HtX_{\rm reg}\cap H_{t}.

Meanwhile, d​ψd\psi vanishes on XsingX_{\rm sing}. Since each HtH_{t} intersects S=XsingS=X_{\rm sing} transversally for each parameter tt and since XsingX_{\rm sing} has codimension at least two in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}, we have that Ht∩XsingH_{t}\cap X_{\rm sing} has codimension at least two in HtH_{t}. We conclude that for t∈𝔻∖𝔻0t\in\mathbb{D}\setminus\mathbb{D}_{0} we have

X∩Ht:={𝒚∈Ht:ψ|Ht​(𝒚)=0}\displaystyle X\cap H_{t}:=\{{\bm{y}}\in H_{t}\,:\,\psi|_{H_{t}}({\bm{y}})=0\}

with d⁡(ψ|Ht)d(\psi|_{H_{t}}) vanishing only on the non-empty subset Ht∩SH_{t}\cap S that has codimension two or higher within HtH_{t}. Therefore, if t∈𝔻∖𝔻0t\in\mathbb{D}\setminus\mathbb{D}_{0} the hyperplane HtH_{t} satisfies Property (1).

We will now show that Property (3) holds for all parameters tt outside of another zero measure subset of 𝔻\mathbb{D}. Because g−1​(Ht)g^{-1}(H_{t}) is smooth for each t∈𝔻t\in\mathbb{D} we have that the family g−1​(Ht)g^{-1}(H_{t}) forms a smooth codimension one holomorphic foliation of U′U^{\prime}. Parameterizing the leaves using a local transversal in U′U^{\prime} we can again use Sard’s Theorem to show that all but a zero measure subset of the leaves g−1​(Ht)g^{-1}(H_{t}) are transverse to the smooth manifold g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X). Such leaves satisfy that g−1​(X)∩g−1​(Ht)g^{-1}(X)\cap g^{-1}(H_{t}) is smooth.

We therefore find the desired hyperplane HH by choosing tt outside of the union of the two measure zero subsets of 𝔻\mathbb{D} that were described in the previous three paragraphs. ∎

Proof of Theorem A.

The proof will be by induction on the dimension nn of the ambient space ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. When n=2n=2, the singular locus of XX must be of dimension 00 and Theorem A follows from Proposition 4.1.

Now suppose that the statement of Theorem A holds when the ambient space has dimension n≥2n\geq 2 in order to prove it for when the ambient space has dimension n+1n+1. Let XX be a germ of a hypersurface at the origin in ℂn+1\mathbb{C}^{n+1} that is singular at 𝟎{\bm{0}}. If 𝟎{\bm{0}} is an isolated singularity for XX, then the result again follows from Proposition 4.1. Meanwhile, if XX is reducible, then the preimage under any finite map is again reducible, and hence singular.

Otherwise, we suppose for contradiction that there does exist a finite holomorphic mapping g:(U,𝟎)→(W,𝟎)g:(U,{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(W,{\bm{0}}) with U,W⊂ℂn+1U,W\subset\mathbb{C}^{n+1} open and an irreducible hypersurface XX with positive dimensional singular locus XsingX_{\rm sing} passing through 𝟎{\bm{0}} such that g−1​(X)g^{-1}(X) is smooth in UU. In this case, Proposition 4.3 will allow us to reduce the dimension of the ambient space by one, in order to contradict the induction hypothesis.

More specifically, Proposition 4.3 gives us open sets U′⊂UU^{\prime}\subset U and W′⊂WW^{\prime}\subset W such that g⁡(U′)=W′g(U^{\prime})=W^{\prime} and a hyperplane HH such that X~:=X∩H\widetilde{X}:=X\cap H is again singular in H∩W′H\cap W^{\prime} but with g−1​(H)g^{-1}(H) smooth in U′U^{\prime} and g−1​(X~)g^{-1}(\widetilde{X}) smooth within g−1​(H)∩U′g^{-1}(H)\cap U^{\prime}. Choosing local coordinates on g−1​(H)g^{-1}(H) and HH, respectively, we obtain a new germ of a finite holomorphic mapping g~:(ℂn,𝟎)→(ℂn,𝟎)\widetilde{g}:(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}})\rightarrow(\mathbb{C}^{n},{\bm{0}}) such that the preimage of a singular hypersurface X~\widetilde{X} is smooth. This violates the induction hypothesis.

We conclude that the statement of Theorem A holds for any dimension ambient space.

∎
